claim: Both is used to explain the equivalence of predicative a nuisance and nuisances with a plural subject, as in Both Ed’s daughters are nuisances / a nuisance [19ii].
evidence_summary: Fix two semicircular tiles arranged edge to edge. “Both tiles together are a complete disk” is true of the pair. “Each tile is a complete disk” is false in that very arrangement. CGEL itself allows a joint reading with both in the piano example on p. 377.
finding: Both can occur with joint attribution. The overt together and the predicate disk make this a control on the proposed explanation. Neither this control nor the behaviour of Ed’s daughters together versus alone decides the equivalence of a nuisance and nuisances in [19ii].
inference: Does both force distributive attribution strongly enough to explain the equivalence in [19ii]?

evidence.passage: §19.3, p. 515, [19ii] and following paragraph. With both, CGEL says the singular and plural nuisance versions “are equivalent”, attributing this to distributivity. Compare §7.3, p. 377, [17i].
